chunks.content: Introduction Severe cutaneous adverse reactions (SCARs) are a group of adverse reactions resulting from drug-induced T cell-mediated hypersensitivity characterized by severe skin eruptions and varying degrees of systemic involvement – . The SCARs category consists of several distinct disease entities, including Stevens–Johnson syndrome (SJS) and toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN) (discussed jointly throughout as SJS/TEN), drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS; also called drug-induced hypersensitivity syndrome (DiHS)), acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis (AGEP), and generalized bullous fixed drug eruption (GBFDE) , – . Whilst certain more severe conditions, such as acquired epidermolysis bullosa, subacute lupus erythematosus or skin vasculitis, have been associated with drug use, this Primer focuses specifically on the disease entities of SJS/TEN, DRESS, AGEP and GBFDE. Despite their rarity, SCARs, especially SJS/TEN, carry significant morbidity and mortality , , , . Early identification and prompt withdrawal of the offending drugs are crucial to minimizing the progression of these life-threatening conditions , , . SJS and TEN are characterized by widespread blistering cutaneous eruptions, atypical targets and extensive mucosal erosions – . SJS/TEN represent distinct clinical entities from erythema multiforme, which manifests with typical targets and a potentially recurrent nature, often linked to infectious aetiology , , . SJS and TEN represent the same disease with differences in the extent of epidermal detachment of total body surface area (<10%, 10–30% and >30% for SJS, SJS–TEN overlap and TEN, respectively) – . SJS/TEN is primarily associated with drug usage (for example, allopurinol, sulfonamides, aromatic anticonvulsants and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs)) in susceptible individuals , . SJS/TEN is characterized by a prominent activation of type 1 cytotoxic T (T c 1) lymphocytes and natural killer cells, corresponding to a type IVa hypersensitivity reaction in the modern nomenclature – . Genetic variants of the human leukocyte antigens (HLA) and drug-metabolizing enzymes are associated with SJS/TEN (for example, HLA-B*15:02 for carbamazepine-induced SJS/TEN , HLA-B*58:01 for allopurinol-induced SCARs , and CYP2C9*3 for phenytoin-induced SCARs) , . Upon the recognition of drug antigens presented by HLA, T c 1 cells are activated to express FAS ligand (FASL) and release cytotoxic proteins (for example, granulysin (GNLY), granzyme B (GZMB) and perforin (PRF1)) from the granules, resulting in keratinocyte death and widespread mucocutaneous necrosis , , , . Intensive care is often required due to extensive epidermal detachment and consequent homeostatic disturbances, infections and inflammation. Survivors frequently suffer from profound functional impairment and psychological trauma. DRESS is a multisystem hypersensitivity reaction with a diffuse, infiltrative maculopapular eruption, visceral organ inflammation and haematological abnormalities – . DRESS is a type IVb reaction, mainly involving T helper 2 (T H 2) lymphocyte activation and viral reactivation , , . In addition to the prominent inflammation in the acute phase, affected individuals are at risk of autoimmune sequelae and multidrug hypersensitivity later in life – . Similar to SJS/TEN, allopurinol, sulfonamides, aromatic anticonvulsants, dapsone and several antimicrobial agents are common culprits for DRESS , , . HLA alleles have been shown to be the risks for DRESS (for example, HLA-B*57:01 for abacavir hypersensitivity , , HLA-A*31:01 for carbamazepine-induced DRESS – , HLA-B*13:01 for dapsone hypersensitivity and HLA-A*32:01 for vancomycin-induced DRESS ). Notably, abacavir hypersensitivity is a unique CD8 + T cell reaction that affects the skin alone in 70% of cases and lacks many of the classical features of DRESS , . Months-long treatment is often required for DRESS due to its protracted nature. AGEP and GBFDE are milder forms of SCARs. AGEP is characterized by abrupt onset of numerous sterile pustules with painful erythema, classically following administration of antibiotics with a short latency period – . GBFDE manifests as rapid onset of widespread erythematous patches and frequently reoccurs at the same sites as previous occurrences . GBFDE is commonly associated with the use of NSAIDs, and the cutaneous lesions can coalesce and form blisters resembling SJS/TEN. However, interspersed areas of normal skin are usually observed in GBFDE. Unlike other forms of SCARs, prior episodes of less extensive reactions are often present in GBFDE. The burden of SCARs is substantial, especially for those enduring lifelong physical complications and psychosocial consequences. Whilst increased awareness of these reactions, implementation of pre-emptive screening programmes and improvement of care have reduced the mortality of SCARs over the past decades, further studies on the disease biomarkers and therapies are needed to address the morbidity and quality of life challenges both in the acute and lifelong settings. In this Primer, we discuss the current understanding of SCARs regarding the epidemiology, pathophysiology, diagnosis, screening, management, and effects on quality of life and address the critical challenges and unmet needs in the field. Epidemiology Stevens–Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis Incidence, risk factors, mortality and complications. SJS/TEN, the most severe and acute form of SCARs, has an incidence of 1–13 cases per million per year for SJS and 0.4–1.2 cases per million per year for TEN – . Reported high incidence rates of SJS/TEN are often derived from analyses using ICD codes in health claims data bases, which are not specifically tailored for the investigation of rare diseases and lack the capacity to review individual cases. By contrast, population-based registries offer data with strictly validated diagnoses, reporting incidence rates of 1–2 cases per million per year , , . In children, estimated incidence rates in the USA were 5.3, 0.8 and 0.4 cases per million per year for SJS, SJS–TEN overlap and TEN, respectively . The higher rates in children are also based on ICD codes of health claims data bases and most likely include many cases of misdiagnosed erythema multiforme major . The global incidence of SJS/TEN has remained stable , – . In people living with HIV who have progressed into acquired immunodeficiency syndrome, the incidence of SJS/TEN is significantly higher, reaching as high as 2 per 1,000 individuals . Older age, especially ≥80 years, is associated with an increased risk of SJS/TEN , . In Germany, the estimated annual incidence rate of SJS/TEN per 1 million individuals per year was reported as 3.01 for those aged ≥80 years compared with 0.66 for individuals aged between 19 and 64 years . Other factors contributing to SJS/TEN risk include underlying malignancies, especially lymphoma, and systemic lupus erythematosus , . A cohort study from the UK reported a twofold higher risk of SJS/TEN in Black and Asian individuals than in white individuals . Notably, there is no significant association between SJS/TEN and factors like body mass index, smoking or alcohol consumption , . The mortality rates usually correspond to the degree of epidermal detachment and vary between <10% in SJS and >40% in TEN, with an overall mortality of ~20% , , , . The mortality is mainly due to sepsis and the prognostic factors include older age (≥65 years), extension of necrolysis, chronic kidney disease (that is, elevation of serum urea and creatinine levels), pneumonia, serum glucose levels and malignant neoplasm – . The mortality rate of SJS/TEN in children is much lower than that in adults; however, approximately half of affected children experience long-term sequelae – . The long-term sequelae of SJS/TEN include ocular complications, nail dystrophy, sicca syndrome, and post-inflammatory hypopigmentation or hyperpigmentation , , – . Associated drugs. A drug is thought to be involved in up to 8 of 10 cases of SJS/TEN , , . Two large case–control studies undertaken in Europe reported the common culprit drugs for SJS/TEN, including allopurinol, antibacterial sulfonamides and sulfasalazine, aromatic antiepileptic medications (carbamazepine, phenytoin, lamotrigine, phenobarbital), NSAIDs of the oxicam type, and the anti-HIV-drug nevirapine , . As indicated in numerous case series worldwide, allopurinol has been identified as the leading cause of SJS/TEN globally; allopurinol is used to lower high blood uric acid levels , , . New exposure to allopurinol for gout was associated with a 20-fold increased risk, and new exposure to carbamazepine (an anticonvulsant) was linked to a fivefold increased risk of SJS/TEN , , . The antibiotic co-trimoxazole (5.37 cases per 10 million defined daily doses) and the antiepileptic drug lamotrigine (3.54 cases per 10 million defined daily doses) have the highest reported incidence rates among individual drugs associated with SJS/TEN . Other antibiotics, including sulfonamides, penicillins, cephalosporins, quinolones and macrolides, were reported to account for 28% of SJS/TEN in a recent meta-analysis . The risk period for a medication to induce SJS/TEN has been identified to be between 4 days and 4 weeks before reaction onset but may be longer, with up to 8 weeks for certain medications, especially those with a long half-life such as allopurinol, phenytoin, carbamazepine or lamotrigine , , , . In addition, the emerging immune-checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), which non-specifically enhance the activity of T lymphocytes, have been reported to trigger SJS/TEN – . Non-drug-induced SJS/TEN is more frequently observed in children, adolescents and young adults compared with elderly patients , . Data from the German Registry show that over 50% of paediatric SJS/TEN cases do not have an identified causative drug . In addition to drugs, infections caused by viruses, mycoplasma and bacteria could serve as triggers for SJS/TEN, although the aetiology of some cases remains unclear , . There is a higher recurrence rate of SJS in children compared with adults, potentially attributable to the greater prevalence of infectious agents associated with SJS in children – . Among paediatric patients, Mycoplasma pneumonia emerges as the predominant infectious cause of SJS/TEN , . Whilst herpes viruses can induce erythema multiforme and SJS, they are not associated with the development of TEN , , . Additionally, 34 cases of SJS/TEN have been reported following infection with SARS-CoV-2 or vaccination against it . Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms Incidence, risk factors, mortality and complications. DRESS is characterized by delayed onset (2–8 weeks) after exposure to the culprit drugs and a prolonged course – . The incidence of DRESS is estimated to be between 1 in 1,000 and 1 in 10,000 depending on the drug culprit – . The prevalence of DRESS was 2.18 per 100,000 in the USA and 9.63 cases per 100,000 in Thailand , . Hepatic, renal and pulmonary involvement are common in DRESS. The mortality rate of DRESS is up to 10% , . Independent predictors of mortality for DRESS are older age (≥57.0 years), kidney involvement and admission to the intensive care unit (ICU) . Paediatric DRESS occurs most commonly in children aged 8 to 10 years , . There does not seem to be any clear differential DRESS risk by sex and ethnicity . Viral reactivations of human herpesvirus 6 (HHV6), HHV7, Epstein–Barr virus (EBV), varicella zoster virus (VZV) or cytomegalovirus (CMV) have been identified during acute DRESS and associated with severe DRESS complications , , , . HHV6 reactivation has been observed in more than one-third of tested paediatric cases from real-world data , . Among patients who have previously experienced DRESS, relapse of the condition occurred in 8.5% of patients and long-term sequelae (for example, autoimmune diseases) occurred in 8.3–16.3% of cases , – . Associated drugs. A prospective study in a multinational registry of SCAR (RegiSCAR) in Europe enroling 201 cases of DRESS from 2003 to mid-2009 revealed that aromatic antiepileptic drugs were the most common culprit drugs (35%; including carbamazepine, phenytoin, lamotrigine, oxcarbazepine and phenobarbital), followed by allopurinol (18%), antibacterial sulfonamides (12%; including sulfasalazine, dapsone, sulfamethoxazole–trimethoprim, sulfadiazine and dapsone), and other antibiotics (11%; including vancomycin, minocycline, amoxicillin and ampicillin–sulbactam) . An analysis of the allergy module of electronic health record data from 1980 to 2016 in the USA identified three primary drug culprits (vancomycin (39%), β-lactams (23%) and anticonvulsants (20%)) as responsible for the majority of DRESS cases . Furthermore, paediatric DRESS cases were most frequently associated with antiepileptics (50%; including carbamazepine, phenytoin, lamotrigine and phenobarbital) and antibiotics (30.8%; particularly vancomycin, trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole and amoxicillin) , . These findings align with an analysis of data from the FDA Adverse Event Reporting System from 2002 to 2019, which identified allopurinol, vancomycin, lamotrigine, carbamazepine and trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole as drugs commonly associated with DRESS . In addition, ICIs can also cause DRESS , . Acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis Incidence, risk factors, mortality and complications. AGEP has an estimated incidence of 1–5 cases per million per year – , – . In a case–control study conducted by EuroSCAR, patients with AGEP were found to have a higher mean age of 56 years and there was a greater proportion of females, with a male-to-female ratio of 0.8, compared to controls with other SCARs . In various case series, the mean age of patients with AGEP was reported as 58 years in the USA , 44 years in Iran and 62 years in Singapore . Although there were variations, a consistent trend of female predominance was observed in these studies, with rates of 73% in Iran, 63% in the USA and 51% in Singapore – . The racial and ethnic distribution of patients with AGEP in the USA study included 61% white, 17% Black or African American, 4% Asian, and 6% Hispanic . Although there were variations, a consistent trend of female predominance was observed in these studies, with rates of 73% in Iran, 63% in the USA and 51% in Singapore – . The racial and ethnic distribution of patients with AGEP in the USA study included 61% white, 17% Black or African American, 4% Asian, and 6% Hispanic . Common comorbidities in patients with AGEP include diabetes and chronic kidney disease, whilst comorbidities such as psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis are rare , . A retrospective review of 340 patients with AGEP across the USA from 2000 to 2020 reported that the all-cause mortality within 30 days was 3.5% . Associated drugs. EuroSCAR reported offending drugs identified in >9 out of 10 cases with AGEP; the strongly associated drugs, that is, drugs within a lower bound of the 95% confidence interval of the odds ratio >5, were pristinamycin, ampicillin–amoxicillin, quinolones, hydroxychloroquine, sulfonamides, terbinafine and diltiazem . Drugs less strongly associated with AGEP were corticosteroids, macrolides other than pristinamycin, NSAIDs and antiepileptic drugs . As pristinamycin use was largely used in France only, it was not identified in studies from other countries , . In addition, iodinated contrast media has also been recognized as a culprit in 19 AGEP cases in France . In a retrospective review of 340 patients in the USA, among the 151 AGEP cases narrowed to a single culprit medication, 63 (41.7%) were β-lactam antimicrobials, 51 (33.8%) were non-β-lactam antimicrobials, 9 (6.0%) were anticonvulsants and 5 (3.3%) were calcium channel blockers . By comparison, a study in Iran assessing 74 AGEP cases reported that the most common drug culprits were hydroxychloroquine, cephalosporin and amoxicillin . In addition, a study in Singapore enroling 43 cases in which a drug was identified (93%), the most common drugs for AGEP were antibiotics (penicillins, cephalosporins and vancomycin) . Generalized bullous fixed drug eruption Incidence, risk factors, mortality, complications and associated drugs. There is no precise incidence rate for GBFDE available. The rates of GBFDE were reported as 3.57% from 952 SCARs cases in the Taiwan Drug-Injury Relief System data collected from 1999 to 2016 (ref. ), and 1.1% from 189 SCARs cases from Malaysia between 2006 and 2015 (ref. ). The risk factors for GBFDE are older age, female sex, prior drug exposure and recurrent fixed drug eruption episodes – . The overall mortality rate has been reported as 11.8–22% , . Complications of GBFDE are infections, fluid loss, dyselectrolytaemia and septicaemia , . The most common causative drugs for GBFDE include paracetamol, NSAIDs, such as mefenamic acid, diclofenac, ibuprofen, ketoprofen and meloxicam, and antibiotics, such as sulfonamides and tetracyclines , , . Global epidemiological differences in SCARs Overall, the most common drugs causing SCARs are allopurinol (the highest single offending agent in Europe, Taiwan, China and the USA) , , , aromatic antiepileptic drugs (the leading cause of SJS/TEN and DRESS in different countries), antimicrobials, certain antiretrovirals and oxicam NSAIDs , , , , , , . SCARs, especially SJS/TEN, particularly in children, are not always associated with drugs but are rather associated with infections, largely viral or bacterial , , . The observed variations in SCAR epidemiology can be attributed, in part, to differential patterns of drug utilization globally as well as differential genetic risks, including HLA alleles and variants in drug metabolism enzymes. For example, in Taiwan and other Southeast Asian countries, a disproportionately higher risk of SJS/TEN was driven by associations with carbamazepine and other aromatic anticonvulsants, which is attributable to genetic susceptibility , , , , . In addition, vancomycin is extensively used in the USA for methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus and co-trimoxazole use is high in sub-Saharan Africa for the treatment of tuberculosis and HIV , , . Beyond drug use and genetic predisposition, other epidemiological risk factors can be helpful for clinical diagnosis and management. Mechanisms/pathophysiology The clinical manifestations of SCARs are indicative of delayed-type T cell-mediated reactions, categorized as type IV hypersensitivity according to the classification by Gell and Coombs , , , . Type IV hypersensitivity is further categorized into IVa, IVb and IVc based on specific T cell subsets, cytokine profiles and subsequent recruitment of leukocytes . SCARs are initiated by the formation of an immune synapse composed of HLA, drug antigen peptide and T cell receptor (TCR) , , . The interaction between drug antigen peptide-bound HLA complexes on antigen-presenting cells and TCRs from different T cell subsets (for example, T c 1, T c 2, and T c 17 lymphocytes and T H 1, T H 2, and T H 17 lymphocytes) is central for initiating these reactions , , . The drug-specific T lymphocytes collaborate between them and recruit other immune cells (for example, type 1, 2 or 3 innate lymphoid cells (ILCs), natural killer cells, macrophages, dendritic cells, eosinophils, B cells, mast cells or basophils, and neutrophils), orchestrating immune responses that result in the clinical heterogeneity of SCARs , , . The pathophysiological mechanisms of SCARs are illustrated in . Stevens–Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis SJS/TEN belongs to type IVa hypersensitivity and has been characterized by the prominent involvement of T c 1 cells, natural killer cells, T H 1 cells and macrophages in blistering skin lesions , , . T c 1 cells and cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs) bearing specific TCRs recognize drug antigens or metabolites (for example, aromatic antiepileptic drugs, allopurinol, sulfonamides, NSAIDs and antibiotics) presented by HLA molecules ( ). The activated T c 1, CTL, natural killer and natural killer T cells produce cytotoxic proteins (for example, GNLY, granzymes (GZMB, GZMA) and PRF1) and death ligands (for example, FASL and TNF), ultimately causing keratinocyte death , , , , , . Other immune cells, including T H 1 cells, ILC1s and macrophages abundant in the skin blisters of SJS/TEN, also release pro-inflammatory cytokines (for example, IL-7, IL-15 and IFNγ), alarmins and death ligands (for example, TNF, annexin A1, TNF superfamily receptor member 12 (TWEAK) and TNF-related apoptosis-inducing ligand (TRAIL)) – . Of note, IL-15 not only maintains the activity of cytotoxic cells but also induces the production of TNF, and its serum levels significantly correlate with disease severity and higher in-hospital mortality of SJS/TEN , . In addition, matrix metalloproteinase 9 (MMP9), induced by TNF, was implicated in epidermal detachment via cleavage of type IV collagen in SJS/TEN . Cytotoxic proteins and death receptor ligation cause extensive keratinocyte death, detachment of the dermo-epidermal junction and full-thickness epidermal necrosis, representing the hallmark features of SJS/TEN ( ). Cell death mechanisms in SJS/TEN. The cell death mechanisms of SJS/TEN are related to the activation of effector cells and massive production of immune mediators in skin lesions, and involve cytotoxic granule-mediated programmed cell death , , , , , apoptosis , , , and necroptosis – ( ). The simultaneous activation of cytotoxic granule-mediated programmed cell death, apoptosis and necroptosis may explain the widespread keratinocyte death observed in SJS/TEN. Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms DRESS is considered a type IVb reaction primarily involving the T H 2 and T c 2 cell immune response , , , . T H 2 and T c 2 cells, which express specific TCRs, recognize drug antigens presented by HLA molecules such as for anticonvulsants, allopurinol, sulfonamides, antibiotics and antiretroviral agents (nevirapine and abacavir) ( ). T H 2 cells express CD134 and produce IL-5, IL-4, IL-10, and IL-13 as well as eotaxin cytokines – . In addition to T H 2 and T c 2 cells, DRESS also involves the activation of regulatory T (T reg ) cells, ILC2s, eosinophils, B cells and dendritic cells , , , . Particularly, the rapid clonal expansion of immunosuppressive T reg cells (specifically CD4 + CD25 + FOXP3 + ) in the acute phase of DRESS plays an important role in its relatively immunocompromised profile, which is characterized by reductions in immunoglobulin levels and peripheral B cell counts and the presence of exhausted antiviral T lymphocytes, therefore facilitating viral reactivation , . Additionally, the Janus kinase (JAK)–STAT signalling pathway and immune mediators such as IFNγ, TNF and thymus and activation-regulated chemokine (TARC)/CCL17 also participate in DRESS pathogenesis , , . These effector cells and immune mediators collectively contribute to the clinical manifestations of DRESS, including eosinophilia, atypical lymphocytosis, lymphadenopathy, multi-organ damage and systemic manifestations. DRESS is frequently associated with virus reactivation, including HHV6, HHV7, EBV, CMV and VZV , , , – . HHV6 reactivation typically occurs transiently, approximately 2–3 weeks after onset, which is often clinically associated with DRESS relapse. In the early phase of DRESS, the latent HHV6 in monocytes/macrophages may become reactivated and infect T H cells through CD134, which is elevated and positively correlates with HHV6 DNA loads, disease severity and the concentrations of chemokines (for example, TARC/CCL17 and IL-5) , . Persistent reactivations of HHV6 and EBV are significant risk factors for the future development of autoimmune diseases after DRESS episodes . Expanded populations of CD8 + T lymphocytes with TCRs recognizing EBV epitopes were detected in the blood and skin of patients with DRESS, and these TCRs may cross-react to self-peptides, leading to the future development of autoimmune diseases . In addition, the culprit drugs triggered EBV production in EBV-transformed B lymphocytes from patients, implying that EBV reactivation might be involved in the pathomechanism of DRESS . Furthermore, CMV reactivation can lead to severe disease and mortality in patients with DRESS undergoing immunosuppressive therapy . Acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis AGEP represents a type IVc reaction characterized by a massive cell infiltrate consisting of neutrophils in pustules and T H 17 cells, ILC3s and T c 17 cells in the dermis and epidermis , , . Drug-specific T lymphocytes are activated upon recognition of drug antigens (for example, aminopenicillins) presented by HLA ( ). T cells and keratinocytes produce cytokines, for example, IL-8, chemokine (C-X-C motif) ligand 8 (CXCL8), IL-22, IL-36α, and granulocyte–macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF), to promote the accumulation of neutrophils in the skin, resulting in sterile pustule formation in the epidermis and systemic neutrophilia , – . Generalized bullous fixed drug eruption GBFDE occurs at the same sites as previous drug eruption through the activation of central memory T (T cm ) lymphocytes and resident memory T (T rm ) lymphocytes . These memory T cells, possibly triggered by prior virus infection, may cross-react to subsequent drug antigens (for example, NSAIDs) presented by HLA ( ). The activated T cm and T rm cells may produce cytokines to attract T c 1 cells and natural killer cells to produce cytotoxic proteins (for example, GNLY, GZMB and FASL) and attract other leukocytes (for example, T reg cells, macrophages and eosinophils) to the skin lesions, leading to the development of GBFDE . The skin lesions of GBFDE exhibit distinct immunological characteristics compared with those of SJS/TEN, with a higher presence of dermal CD4 + cells, including FOXP3 + T reg cells, fewer intraepidermal natural killer cells, and fewer intraepidermal GNLY + cells. These factors may represent heterologous immunity, explaining the less progressive nature of GBFDE compared with SJS/TEN . Mechanistic models for drug recognition in SCARs The pivotal role of T cells in SCARs has been suggested by the identification of drug-specific T lymphocytes with antigen specificity and HLA restriction. Different mechanistic models have been proposed to explain how T lymphocytes recognize drug antigens, which include the hapten–pro-hapten theory , – , the concept of pharmacological interaction with immune receptors (p-i) , , and an altered peptide repertoire , . In addition, ICI-induced SCARs involve drug antigen-independent T cell overactivation ( and ). These models together with the systemic factors (for example, HLA genetic predisposition, impaired drug metabolism, immune recognition and activation, and heterologous immunity) have been proposed to complete the puzzle of the development of SCARs ( ). HLA as genetic predisposition for SCARs Genetic susceptibility associated with HLA alleles has been extensively documented across diverse ethnic populations, with prominent examples summarized in and . These HLA alleles serve as key determinants in the development of SCARs , . Importantly, these SCAR-associated HLA alleles are not only genetically associated with SCARs but have also been functionally validated as contributors to the presentation of drug antigens to T cells – . This facilitates the presentation of drug antigens to specific T lymphocytes – . Notably, these binding responses exhibit drug-specific and HLA-restricted patterns – . Structural analyses, including crystallography, molecular docking and site-directed mutagenesis, have supported the notion that drugs and their metabolites form covalent or non-covalent interactions with key residues within the HLA groove , – ( ). HLA therefore plays a pivotal role in the pathomechanisms of SCARs. Impaired drug metabolism in SCARs Increased drug antigen levels may enhance the formation of the immune synapse, thus contributing to, facilitating and amplifying SCARs ( ). Elevated concentrations of drug antigens may arise from various factors, including genetic variations in metabolic enzymes or transporters, liver or renal function deficiency, or drug–drug interactions. For instance, the genetic variant CYP2C9*3 disrupts the metabolism of phenytoin, leading to elevated drug plasma levels and an increased risk of phenytoin-induced SCARs , , , . Genetic variants in CYP2B6 and glutathione transferase GSTM1 have been linked to nevirapine-induced SJS/TEN – . Both the HLA-B*58:01 allele and oxypurinol dose are necessary for the induction of a drug-specific T cell response , , . Patients with renal insufficiency (for example, chronic kidney disease) have elevated plasma levels of oxypurinol as well as an increased risk and poorer prognosis for allopurinol-induced SCARs – . The coexistence of HLA-B*58:01 and renal impairment has been reported to further amplify the risk and predictive accuracy of allopurinol-induced SCARs (the odds ratio for heterozygous HLA-B*58:01 and normal renal function is 15.25 and for homozygous HLA-B*58:01 and severe renal impairment is 1269.45) . Furthermore, allopurinol and oxypurinol may non-covalently enhance the binding of self-peptides or viral peptides of EBNA3B to HLA-B*58:01 , which has the potential to trigger the anti-self reactions in SCARs . Immune recognition and activation in SCARs When T lymphocytes bearing specific TCR clonotypes engage with drug antigen-bound HLAs on antigen-presenting cells and keratinocytes, these cells are activated to produce cytokines, chemokines, alarmins and cytotoxic proteins within the skin microenvironment. Heterologous immunity contributes to SCARs Heterologous immunity generated from genetic polymorphisms, the unique immune histories of individuals, underlying diseases, pre-existing pathogen-specific T cells, and viral reactivations or infections contribute to the development and prognosis of SCARs ( ). Infections caused by mycoplasma or viruses (for example, HHV, herpes simplex virus, EBV, CMV, coxsackievirus A6 variant, SARS-CoV-2), vaccination, and systemic diseases have been documented to induce SCARs or reactions resembling the clinical presentation and to intensify the severity of SCARs , . Previously sensitized T cells (for example, T rm , T cm and effector memory T cells) could make up a significant proportion of the memory pool and cross-react with neoantigens generated upon subsequent drug exposure . These T cells can recognize both pathogen peptide-MHC immunogens and drug antigens through molecular mimicry, with neither HLA restriction nor peptide sequence homology serving as prerequisites for the development of heterologous immunity . Moreover, the numbers of T reg cells in the skin lesions (for example, absent or scarce in SJS/TEN, present in GBFDE, and abundant in DRESS) are also likely contributors to heterologous immunity, explaining the different pathological mechanisms and clinical manifestations of various disease entities of SCARs. Diagnosis, screening and prevention Patient history and physical examination The diagnosis of a suspected drug reaction relies on recognizing the characteristic mucocutaneous and systemic manifestations, coupled with a meticulous review of the chronology of drug exposure and symptom evolution ( ). Typically, the clinical course spans 1–2 weeks for AGEP and GBFDE, ~2–3 weeks for SJS/TEN (longer for fatal TEN cases), and 2 weeks to several months for DRESS. The typical primary lesions of SJS/TEN present as an acute onset of widespread painful macules and flat atypical target lesions with central blistering reminiscent of erythema multiforme that rapidly coalesce, resulting in extensive epidermal detachment ( , ). By contrast, erythema multiforme major is distinguished by an acral distribution of raised typical targets, mucosal erosions and <10% skin detachment, with the majority of cases attributed to herpes simplex virus or mycoplasma infections , . Establishing drug causality A comprehensive review of drug history is crucial to establish the chronological relationship between drug exposure and the onset of drug reactions. However, clinical history alone may not be sufficient to identify the culprit agents in most cases. For SJS/TEN, the algorithm of drug causality for epidermal necrolysis (ALDEN) aids in the assessment of potential causative agents . The clinical tool considers the latency periods, quality of the potential culprit drugs (including half-life and notoriety), impact of drug challenge and withdrawal, and the presence or absence of alternative causes. Confirmation of the offending agents As SCARs are a T cell-mediated immune memory response, lifelong avoidance of the suspected triggers and potentially cross-reactive medications are necessary. Confirmation of the responsible agents in SCAR cases is challenging; in particular, drug rechallenge tests are inapplicable in patients with SJS/TEN (due to the lethal nature of SJS/TEN) . Following a clinical diagnosis, the causative agents for SCARs may be determined through in vivo patch or prick tests and ex vivo or in vitro laboratory-based tests – . However, none of these methods provides a 100% negative predictive value (NPV), implying that a negative test result may be a false negative, potentially leading to SCARs in susceptible individuals upon secondary exposure to the causative agents . Combining genetic and functional research studies may help to improve the accuracy . In vivo testing, though generally avoided for SJS/TEN, can be used in understanding the drug causality and specific cross-reactivity patterns in DRESS and AGEP . The reagents and concentrations used for in vivo testing usually represent the highest non-irritating levels . The sensitivity of tests varies widely, from 0% for allopurinol to over 50% for certain anticonvulsants , , . Prick or intradermal tests for the culprits of DRESS showed a sensitivity of 58–67% . In vitro methods, like the lymphocyte transformation test and lymphocyte activation test, and ex vivo tests like enzymelinked immunoSpot (ELISpot) are limited in availability and validation and are primarily used in research laboratories , , , . In addition, the appropriate timing of in vitro testing is critical and related to the SCAR phenotype , . For example, the lymphocyte transformation test should be performed later (≥30 days after onset) in the disease course of DRESS . Recent studies indicate that ELISpot exhibits higher sensitivity and specificity, particularly for DRESS, in comparison to the lymphocyte transformation test , . More understanding of relevant drug antigens, genetic susceptibility and drug–immune receptor interactions can significantly improve diagnostic accuracy and testing performance , . Screening and prevention of SCARs Although many of the above-described genetic associations have been reproduced by more than one group, few of these have been translated directly into clinical practice as preventive tests . A prospective genetic study involving 1,956 patients from 19 countries demonstrated that HLA-B*57:01 screening significantly reduced the risk of abacavir hypersensitivity . The patch test helped define both the high specificity and 100% NPV of HLA-B*57:01 screening for abacavir hypersensitivity across diverse populations . The positive predictive value (PPV) of HLA-B*57:01 for abacavir hypersensitivity was 47.6–76.3%, and the number of patients needed to test (NNT) to prevent one case would be 14–42 (refs. 185–188). HLA-B*57:01 screening for abacavir hypersensitivity has been reality tested in clinical practice as a successful screening strategy and the adverse reaction has been essentially eliminated with pre-prescription testing , . For HLA-B*15:02 and carbamazepine-induced SJS/TEN, this link has been well-established and extensively studied, particularly in Southeast Asian populations, where a near 100% NPV has been observed. However, it is important to note that HLA-B*15:02 does not predict carbamazepine-induced DRESS , . The assets for ‘primary prevention’ of a SCAR include a quality-assured inexpensive test, the availability of safe and effective medication alternatives, and easing clinical practice and shared patient decision-making. Immune-related adverse events Adverse cutaneous reactions associated with ICIs are a relatively novel entity. These reactions, termed immune-related adverse events (irAEs), are characterized by a relatively delayed onset with an unpredictable and often protracted clinical course. The putative molecular mechanisms of these reactions involve self-reactive T cells in the skin . Unlike SCARs caused by small-molecule drugs, irAEs often do not recur on ICI rechallenge. This phenomenon may be attributed to its unique pathomechanism involving T cell overactivation, devoid of ICI drug antigen recognition . The histopathology is often lichenoid and distinct HLA associations have not been described . In addition, lichenoid bullous eruptions, SJS/TEN and DRESS may occur in the setting of ICI-related adverse events , , . Patients are treated according to severity, with lower-grade eruptions treated supportively with or without systemic corticosteroids, whilst interruption of cancer immunotherapy is often required for higher-grade reactions. Additional steroid-sparing immunomodulatory therapy targeting the presumed immunophenotype is also efficacious and can help mitigate the potentially adverse effects of systemic corticosteroids on antitumour immunity – . Successful use of biologic agents and small molecules in managing dermatological irAEs have been described, including IgE blockade with omalizumab to reduce pruritus , anti-IL-17 or anti-IL-23 agents and apremilast to ameliorate psoriasiform eruptions , and the anti-IL-4/IL-13 agent dupilumab to manage type 2 inflammatory reactions . Given the urgency of cancer treatment, rechallenge upon resolution of high-grade dermatological irAEs is not strictly contraindicated . Quality of life Currently, there is a lack of tools precisely designed to assess the quality of life in patients with SCARs. The Drug Hypersensitivity Quality of Life Questionnaire, introduced in 2011, comprises 15 items intended to evaluate the perceived burden of previous drug hypersensitivity in the daily life of patients – . The questionnaire predominantly focuses on the psychological aspects, such as drug aversion and associated anxiety, and does not consider potential long-term physical sequelae of SCARs. These sequelae often result in profound distress and limitations for patients with SCARs, underscoring the need for tools that comprehensively address both the psychological and physical dimensions of their quality of life. Quality of life after the acute phase: SJS/TEN The overall mortality of SJS/TEN is estimated to range from 15% to 20% , , , . Approximately one-third of patients require mechanical ventilation in the ICU , , , . To date, the cornerstone of management is optimized supportive care in reference centres , . After the acute phase, multiple long-term sequelae affect the majority of survivors and have a significant impact on the quality of life. Common sequelae, reported by over half of patients, are cutaneous (pigmentation disorders, scaring, photosensitivity, skin pain), ocular (from dryness to permanent conjunctival inflammation, symblepharons and corneal defects that may lead to blindness), and psychological distress (from anxiety, depression, sleep troubles and fear of any medication to long-term post-traumatic stress disorder in 25–30% of cases) , . A study conducted in a reference centre for SCARs interviewed 57 survivors of SJS/TEN by phone 4 years after the acute phase, and long-term sequelae were reported in 90% of survivors . It found that 53.6% of survivors had a high score of anxiety, 31.6% requested a financial allocation for disability, 45.6% reported a change in employment status, 21.1% had a change in their family life, and some of them declared a high amount of non-reimbursed health expenditure . A recent Taiwanese registry-based study confirmed the lifetime burden of the disease as shown by high health expenditure per year as well as a significant (almost 10-year) reduction in life expectancy, in which sequelae themselves were an independent risk factor . Quality of life after the acute phase: DRESS Compared with SJS/TEN, patients with other SCAR phenotypes tend to have less severe complications and sequelae. However, ~10% of patients with DRESS may develop autoimmune sequelae, such as diabetes, thyroid disorders and vitiligo, which can result in significant psychological distress and drug aversion and can occur up to 5 years post initial DRESS presentation , – . Aside from consultation with an allergist, immunologist and/or dermatologist, patients should be informed about the risk of developing autoimmune diseases and screened for endocrine dysfunction based on clinical suspicion at follow-up. Outlook Culprit agent identification In real-world scenarios, identifying the culprit agents based on clinical history alone is often challenging in SCAR cases, especially those involving multiple drug usage, preceding systemic infections, or underlying hepatic or renal insufficiency that may impact drug clearance. In vivo testing methods are generally contraindicated in SCARs due to the heightened risk of life-threatening reactions upon rechallenge; in vitro methods are currently only available in some specialized centres and research laboratories, necessitating further standardization protocols, skilled laboratory personnel and guided interpretation. Furthermore, these methods still exhibit low sensitivity and specificity for some wellknown culprits like allopurinol . There is an urgent need to enhance the methodology, sample at optimal timing and implement adjunctive measures to refine these aspects, ultimately contributing to improved accuracy in determining the drug causality of SCARs. Early diagnosis and improved prognostication Developing a globally validated diagnostic tool for DRESS is an urgent requirement. In addition, standardized biomarkers for early detection and precise measurement of disease activity in SCARs are currently lacking. Integration of biological markers into the clinical work-up is limited by the accessibility of laboratory resources and largely restricted to specialized centres. For example, blister fluid GNLY level is a potential diagnostic and disease severity marker in patients with SJS/TEN , . Serum GNLY may also aid in the identification of patients at risk of development of SJS/TEN . Identification, validation and implementation of biomarkers, such as serum GNLY, can aid in early diagnosis and refined treatment strategies according to disease activity. Genetic screening and prevention Ongoing identification of specific genetic associations with SCARs has led to the establishment of clinical utility and screening guidelines. Notably, the guidelines provided by the FDA and the Clinical Pharmacogenetics Implementation Consortium have delineated recommendations for the following pharmacogenomic associations: (1) abacavir hypersensitivity syndrome and HLA-B*57:01 (refs. , – ); (2) allopurinol-induced SCARs and HLA-B*58:01 (refs. , , , , ); (3) carbamazepine-induced SJS/TEN and HLA-B*15:02 in people with Asian ancestry , , , ; (4) oxcarbazepine-induced SJS/TEN and HLA-B*15:02 (refs. , ); (5) carbamazepine-induced DRESS and HLA-A*31:01 (refs. , , , ); and (6) phenytoin-induced SCARs and HLA-B*15:02 and CYP2C9*3 (refs. , , , , ). The Clinical Pharmacogenetics Implementation Consortium Guidelines not only provide screening recommendations but also practical therapy suggestions, including dose adjustments when drug use is not contraindicated. Despite these advancements, the practical implementation of pharmacogenomics faces obstacles such as the absence of large-scale prospective trials validating improved outcomes through widespread genotyping, regulatory challenges and a lack of cost-effectiveness analyses across diverse populations. In addition, clinical application of the genetic findings in SCARs has been hindered by low PPV – , , . Efforts to identify susceptible genetic loci and cost-effectiveness assessment of identified genetic associations are needed to facilitate the implementation of screening programmes and investigate their generalizability across populations. Furthermore, with the marketing of newer therapeutics, such as ICIs and various small-molecule inhibitors, pharmacovigilance registries are instrumental to identifying high-risk medications and susceptible populations. Precision management Despite tremendous progress in understanding the disease pathogenesis and genetic risk factors, there is a lack of evidence-based supportive care and treatment options to derive the best clinical management for SCARs. Key issues include optimal mucocutaneous care for patients with SJS/TEN, ideal treatment and follow-up duration to mitigate the risk of recurrence and minimize long-term sequelae with DRESS, and timing and duration of immunomodulatory therapy in different SCAR phenotypes to maximize treatment benefit and minimize adverse effects. An individualized strategy based on disease phase and activity may be needed to provide tailored therapy for each patient, which requires more precise assessment of disease activity and improved prediction of disease course on an individual level. To address these gaps in management, prospective studies on a larger scale are warranted to inform clinical practice. Pathophysiology-guided therapy Understanding the pathophysiology behind SCARs is crucial for identifying new cellular and molecular therapeutic targets. It is still unclear why T cell-mediated hypersensitivity reactions to drugs occur so frequently in the skin. It may be related to the fact that skin is a metabolically active and immune-competent organ, capable of generating various metabolites and antigens and attracting diverse immune cells and mediators , . Furthermore, as an important barrier to the external environment, skin is also capable of launching a rapid immune response upon exogenous insults and endogenous danger signals , . Comprehensive studies based on well-organized sample collection for rare cases and temporal assessment of different clinical presentations at various phases of disease are needed. In addition, treatment options for the precise targeting of distinct pathophysiological pathways are limited. For example, none of the existing therapies can effectively modulate the cell death pathways in SJS/TEN. Further studies are needed to understand the critical drivers of disease progression in the early phase of SCARs and to develop interventions that can arrest the progression and potentially prevent the development of SCARs. Lastly, as new irAEs emerge, further studies are warranted to investigate the detailed immunological mechanisms and explore potential prophylactic and management strategies. These efforts are essential for advancing our understanding and enhancing therapeutic approaches to mitigate the impact of SCARs. Global collaboration Whilst certain similarities are observed among subtypes of SCARs, such as the high-risk causative drugs (for example, allopurinol, aromatic antiepileptics like carbamazepine, phenytoin, lamotrigine and some antibiotics) and the common genetic risk factors (for example, HLA-B*58:01 and allopurinol-induced SCARs, CYP2C9*3 and phenytoin-induced SCARs) shared between SJS/TEN and DRESS, there are still notable variations in SCAR characteristics. For instance, a nationwide study comprising 745 SCAR cases from a multicentre registry in Korea revealed that SJS/TEN was observed most frequently following the use of carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (100%), NSAIDs (84%) and acetaminophen (83%), whereas dapsone (100%), anti-tuberculous agents (81%) and glycopeptide antibacterials (78%) were more likely to cause DRESS . Beyond nationwide studies, the rarity of SCARs emphasizes the urgent need for an international research alliance. Such collaboration holds the potential to facilitate the establishment of large-scale pharmacovigilance registries and studies focusing on new prognostic and therapeutic strategies. Coordinated efforts can lead to the development of comprehensive multidisciplinary and international practice guidelines, addressing the challenges posed by the complex conditions of SCARs.
